    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30163v1</id>
    <title>ReVAgent: Multi-Agent Reasoning-Intensive Video Generation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T07:11:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30163v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30163v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A central challenge in generating instructional videos for reasoning-intensive topics is to show how and why the state changes at each step. Even when an animation renders successfully, the depicted object relationships and state transitions can conflict with the explanation, making the reasoning difficult to follow. We present ReVAgent, a multi-agent framework that solves a problem, generates keyframes for its explanation, and synthesizes an instructional video. The agents share the execution record of a solution program, reuse intermediate results and constructions in the scenes, and check rendered keyframes to guide revisions to the solution or the scenes. We also introduce a multidimensional rubric for assessing whether generated videos present the problem clearly, organize the steps coherently, and use visuals to explain the reasoning. We calibrate a multimodal judge using human ratings and apply it to instructional videos for mathematics and algorithms. In the evaluated samples, ReVAgent presents multi-step reasoning coherently and uses diagrams to show how key operations lead to subsequent states.</summary>
    <category term="cs.AI" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30035v1</id>
    <title>TRAE: Trustworthy Automated ESG Annotation via Multi-Agent Consensus and Confidence Assessment</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T04:44:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30035v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30035v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>With the growing demand for ESG disclosure and evaluation, constructing high-quality datasets for automatically extracting ESG-related information from large-scale documents has become essential. However, ESG annotation remains challenging due to strong context dependence, ambiguous label boundaries, and the need for domain expertise, resulting in high annotation cost and limited scalability. To address these challenges, we propose TRAE (TRustworthy Automated ESG annotation), a multi-agent framework for scalable and reliable ESG data construction. Unlike direct LLM-based annotation, TRAE evaluates annotation reliability by modeling agreement, confidence, and reasoning consistency among multiple agents through a structured multi-step reasoning process. Experimental results demonstrate that TRAE improves annotation performance compared with existing automated annotation strategies. Furthermore, TRAE supports a hybrid human-AI annotation strategy that assigns expert labeling only to uncertain samples, reducing annotation cost while preserving data quality. Using TRAE, we construct a high-quality ESG dataset containing approximately 20,000 instances with complete reasoning traces, intermediate agent outputs, and reliability information to enhance transparency and reproducibility. Overall, this work provides a practical and scalable framework for trustworthy ESG data construction. The code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/nowzer0/TRAE.</summary>
    <category term="cs.MA" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29457v1</id>
    <title>MAS-BIT: A Multi-Agent System for End-to-End BraIn-to-Text Decoding</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T12:55:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29457v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29457v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Speech brain-computer interfaces aim to restore communication by translating neural activity into text, yet end-to-end decoders have historically trailed cascaded systems in accuracy. We introduce a Multi-Agent System for BraIn-to-Text (MAS-BIT), the first multi-agent framework for end-to-end brain-to-text decoding from intracortical recordings. MAS-BIT coordinates three specialized agents: a neural agent that interprets continuous neural representations, a phonetic agent that decodes soft phoneme posteriors, and an arbitration agent that integrates their complementary evidence with direct access to neural representations to generate the final transcription. The expert agents communicate with the arbiter through token-embedding-based latent communication, constructing continuous messages as probability-weighted combinations of token embeddings. These messages retain alternative token hypotheses and provide a differentiable interface through which sentence-level supervision jointly trains the neural encoders and specialized agents across participants. MAS-BIT achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end decoding performance on the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, with word error rates of 6.929% on '24 and 3.606% on the '25 public test set (3.892% on the private test set). These results surpass the published BIT cascade on the '25 public set and narrow the gap on '24, without ensembling independently trained models or using external language-model rescoring.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29248v1</id>
    <title>AgenticMM: A Material-Centered Multi-Agent Architecture for Scalable First-Principles Materials Modeling</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T05:40:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29248v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29248v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent frameworks are attracting increasing attention as a means of autonomously driving complex, long-running workflows in first-principles materials modeling. However, such frameworks commonly organize AI agents by computational task or scientific role. When scaled across many materials, this organization can require repeated transfers of material-specific context and complicate persistent execution and resource coordination. Here, we introduce AgenticMM, a material-centered multi-agent architecture in which each material has a persistent agent that owns its complete workflow and retains its scientific context, while a persistent coordinator allocates shared resources, mediates communication, and tracks campaign progress. AgenticMM is designed to incorporate reusable, prompt-based skills as modular definitions of these workflows. Using DefectSkills prompts, we demonstrate the feasibility of AgenticMM through a multistage point-defect campaign in which material-specific agents concurrently perform host electronic-structure, phase-stability, and intrinsic-defect calculations for five chemically diverse semiconductors.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28617v1</id>
    <title>VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:09:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28617v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28617v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.</summary>
